note_on_method: Each venue page rests on two Louisville Parks and Recreation pages - the pickleball page, whose "Pickleball Court List:" gives one line per park in the form "Vettiner Park - 14" and introduces the whole set as outdoor, and the park's own page, which gives a "Park Address", a year acquired, a size in acres, "Hours" of "6 a.m. - 11 p.m." and an amenity list in which Pickleball is a word without a number. The US Census address geocoder and OpenStreetMap supply the county and the postcode, and because Louisville is a consolidated city-county they name the city three ways. Where the City is silent - on lighting, price, surface, nets and parking, at every venue - these pages record the silence.

slots.description:
Fourteen outdoor pickleball courts, the largest set in Louisville by a distance, on one line of the City's pickleball page: "Vettiner Park - 14". The next largest count in the city is six, at four parks, so this one venue holds more than a fifth of the sixty-seven courts verified across the city. The park's own page calls it Charlie Vettiner Park - the list drops the first name - and lists "Pickleball" among its amenities without a number, so the fourteen rests on the list and the park page confirms that the courts exist.

The park is 283 acres, acquired in 1957, and its amenity list is one of the longest in the city: ballfields, baseball, basketball, cross country, disc golf, a dog run, fishing, golf, grills, a hiking trail, a memorial, model airplane flying fields, a multi-purpose field, passive open space, pickleball, picnic shelters, a playground, restrooms, tennis, walking and WiFi. The page links a "Guide for Model Airplane & Model Helicopter Flying", the only activity the City writes a guide for here. The courts are one feature among many on a large site.
slots.getting_there:
5550 Charlie Vettiner Park Rd, Louisville, KY 40299. The address resolves through OpenStreetMap rather than the US Census address file, which holds no record of it; OpenStreetMap matches "5550, Charlie Vettiner Park Road, Louisville, Jefferson County, Kentucky, 40299" at house-number level and names the place "Louisville", one of the three names the resolvers use for the consolidated city. The City's page prints 40299 and the resolver agrees.

The City publishes nothing about parking. Restrooms are on the amenity list. The address is a park road named for the park, and on a 283-acre site it locates the park rather than the courts; the City does not say where inside it they are.
slots.what_to_expect:
Fourteen courts is a rotation that absorbs a crowd, and it makes this the one Louisville venue where turning up alone is a reasonable plan on the count. Whether a rotation actually forms, and when, is not something the City publishes - no open-play session, no schedule, no group is named anywhere on its pickleball page - so that remains an inference from the number rather than a fact from the operator.

The park is open "6 a.m. - 11 p.m." on its own page. Those are park hours: the City states nothing about lighting here or anywhere in Louisville, and this site does not read a court usable at ten at night into a gate that closes at eleven. Price is not stated, and the City's mention of rentals on its pickleball page carries no figure. Surface is not stated. Nets are not stated. The courts are outdoor on the City's own sentence introducing the list. What the City does put beside the courts is a large park - a golf course, a dog run, disc golf, fishing and fields for model aircraft - which says the site is busy with other things and nothing about the courts.

faqs.a: Fourteen, on the City's list: "Vettiner Park - 14". The park's own page lists pickleball among its amenities without a count. It is the largest set in Louisville.
Not stated. The park is open until 11 p.m. on its page, but the City says nothing about lighting at any Louisville venue, so this site records it as unverified.
Not stated. The City publishes no price for any pickleball court in Louisville, and this site does not assume a park court is free.
"6 a.m. - 11 p.m." under "Hours" on the park's own page. Every Louisville park page prints the same line, and it is the park's hours rather than the courts'.

faqs.a: The US Census address file holds no record of 5550 Charlie Vettiner Park Rd. OpenStreetMap matches it at house-number level in Jefferson County and names the place Louisville.

slots.description:
Four outdoor pickleball courts in the oldest park on this site's Louisville pages, from the City's line "Iroquois - 4". The park page gives the full name, Iroquois Park, and describes it in the City's own words: "planned by Frederick Law Olmsted as a 'scenic reservation' of forested hillsides and breathtaking vistas", with "the WPA-era Iroquois Amphitheater, an open-air theater that accommodates 2,366 people". A tulip poplar in the park is, the City says, believed to be the largest in its parks system.

The park was acquired in 1888 and is 725.85 acres, the second largest published venue in Louisville after McNeely Lake. Its amenity list runs to an amphitheatre, archery, basketball, road biking, disc golf, a futsal court, golf, grills, a hiking trail, horse riding trails, a horseshoe pit, a multi-purpose field, pickleball, picnic shelters, a playground, restrooms, a sprayground, tennis, volleyball, walking, a wheelchair-accessible playground and WiFi. Pickleball is one word on that list, without a count; the four is the pickleball page's.

No second resolver was needed, and the City's postcode and the Census's agree.

The City publishes nothing about parking. On a park of over seven hundred acres the address is an entrance, not the courts, and the City's page does not say where inside the park the courts are. Restrooms are on the amenity list.
slots.what_to_expect:
Four courts is two games at once, or a group of eight rotating without much waiting. The City publishes no session, no schedule and no rotation rule, so who is on the courts and when is not on the record.

Hours are "6 a.m. - 11 p.m." on the park page, the same line every Louisville park carries; they are park hours, and lighting is not stated, so evening play is an open question rather than a yes. Price is not stated. Surface is not stated. Nets are not stated. The courts are outdoor because the City's list introduces every count as an outdoor count.

What is stated is the setting, and the City is unusually willing to describe it: an Olmsted park of forested hillsides, an amphitheatre for 2,366, riding trails and a golf course. Of the sixteen venues on this site's Louisville pages only Iroquois, McNeely Lake and Hays Kennedy get more than a line of description from the City; the rest get an address, a year, a size and a list. Expect a court that is a small part of a very large park.

Two outdoor pickleball courts in the largest park published in Louisville, from the City's line "McNeely Lake - 2". The park page describes it as "one of the largest in the Metro Parks system", 746 acres, acquired in 1961, with "a scenic 46-acre fishing lake with an accessible pier and boat ramp which is owned by the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife" and the Korean War Memorial. The page links a park map and guide and a guide to model airplane and helicopter flying.

Two courts is a game rather than a rotation: a four can play, an eight will wait, and if both courts are taken there is nowhere else at this address to go. The amenity list is long - ballfields, basketball, boat ramps, canoe access, cross country, fishing, golf, grills, a hiking trail, horse riding trails, model airplane flying fields, a multi-purpose field, passive open space, pickleball, picnic shelters, a playground, a pond, restrooms, tennis and walking - and pickleball is one word on it, without a number. The count is the pickleball page's alone, and the park page confirms the courts exist.

With two courts and no published session, this is a venue for a pair or a four who arrive together, not for joining a game. What McNeely Lake has that those do not is the rest of the park - a 46-acre lake with an accessible pier, a golf course, riding and hiking trails, fields for model aircraft and a memorial - which the City describes and the courts do not change. The park was acquired in 1925 and is 77 acres, and its address is on Reservoir Avenue. Its amenity list is short for a Louisville park: golf, pickleball, picnic shelter, picnic table, playground, sprayground, swimming, tennis and WiFi. Pickleball is one word on that list without a count; the four is the pickleball page's.

What is not on the list matters as much. Crescent Hill is one of three published Louisville venues whose park page does not list restrooms - George Rogers Clark and New Walnut Street are the others - and this site records that as unknown rather than as a no, because the City's amenity lists are not written as complete inventories. Four courts is two games at once, or eight players rotating without a long wait; it puts Crescent Hill level with Iroquois, Petersburg and Riverview in the middle of Louisville's table.

Four courts is a workable number without being a complex - enough for two games, or for a group of eight to rotate - and the City publishes no session or open-play time here, so bring your own game. The pickleball page says six; the park page says nothing; the six publishes, because a stated count on the operator's own list is the fact this site requires, and the silence is recorded beside it.

The silence is also asserted. The build that makes this page re-reads the park page on every run and fails the day the word pickleball appears on it, so this caveat cannot outlive its truth. Six courts is enough for a rotation to form, and it puts Fern Creek level with Hays Kennedy, Wyandotte and Nelson Hornbeck as the second-largest count in the city.

Its amenity list is ballfields, basketball, a cricket pitch, grills, a multi-purpose field, pickleball, picnic shelters, a playground, restrooms, river frontage, tennis, walking and WiFi; pickleball is on it without a number, and the six is the pickleball page's.
